title: Bloom-guided lazy restore and zero-copy KV overlay for paged attention
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Problem: With paged attention we evict and restore KV pages frequently during bursty workloads. Full-page prefill causes excessive bandwidth, long prefill latencies, and wasted decode work when only a small subset of slots in a page is accessed by the incoming token stream. Existing heuristics either over-prefill (waste) or under-prefill (tail latency).

Proposal: Introduce a Bloom-guided lazy-restore flow + zero-copy KV overlay that enables kernels to operate on a mixed-residency page without requiring full materialization. Key ideas: (1) Maintain a compact Bloom filter per evicted page that approximates which token keys (or key spans) were resident recently; (2) On prefill, consult the Bloom to perform a targeted, slot-level restore into a small ephemeral reservoir backed by GPU memory; (3) Expose a zero-copy overlay mapping that merges restored slots, resident slots, and placeholder zeros so the attention kernel can read a coherent view without copying the entire page; (4) Add kernel-selection heuristics to choose a sparse-aware kernel vs dense kernel depending on overlay density and request latency budget; (5) Use an ephemeral reservoir with soft-residency so very-hot micro-slices can be promoted without moving whole pages, reducing thrash.

Why this is different: Instead of trying to predict access at the request-level with heavy ML predictors or expensive per-slot metadata, the Bloom approach keeps a compact probabilistic summary that is cheap to read and update on eviction. The zero-copy overlay avoids host/GPU copy amplification and integrates with existing attention kernels by providing a unified read abstraction. Kernel selection avoids one-size-fits-all: sparse kernels (lower memory but higher per-slot overhead) are preferable for low-density overlays while dense kernels win on high-density restores.

Implementation plan (high level):
1) Data model: define per-page Bloom layout (size, hash functions) and eviction-time Bloom population rules. Store Bloom metadata alongside page metadata in the KV manager.
2) Overlay API: implement a read-only overlay view for the GPU kernel that composes resident page pointers, ephemeral reservoir pointers, and zero-fill placeholders. Keep the overlay descriptor compact for fast kernel startup.
3) Reservoir allocator: small LRU/GDS-backed reservoir for ephemeral restored slots; implement admission policy (thresholds, promotion rules).
4) Kernel changes: add a thin adapter in the attention runtime to accept overlay descriptors and select sparse/dense kernels based on a cheaply computable density estimate. Add branch for fallback to full prefill if overlay density exceeds safe threshold.
5) Prefill flow: on cache miss, consult Bloom to obtain candidate slot set, restore only those slots asynchronously into reservoir, return early to user with overlay mapping. Provide optional synchronous path for low-severity requests.
6) Metrics & tracing: instrument false-positive rate, restored bytes per request, overlay density distribution, tail-latency percentiles, and eviction/promotion churn.
7) Safety and multi-tenant isolation: ensure Bloom metadata cannot leak tenant values; reservoir is per-tenant and admission respects tenant weights. Provide auditable accounting for restored bytes.

Trade-offs and risks:
- Bloom false positives will cause extra restores; we can tune Bloom size vs FPR. Low FPR requires more metadata bytes per page.
- Overlay complexity in kernel increases code surface and maintenance burden. We will hide complexity behind a stable overlay descriptor ABI.
- Reservoir eviction policy can introduce subtle fairness issues; we must integrate with tenant-weighted residency quotas.
- Some workloads (dense access patterns) will trigger full prefill fallback, reducing benefit; detection heuristics must be conservative to avoid repeated fallbacks.

Measurement targets (hypothesis):
- Reduce average restored bytes per cache miss by 40–70% on sparse workloads.
- Reduce 99.9th decode latency from prefill storms by 20–50% in mixed workloads.
- Keep additional per-page metadata under 256 bytes (configurable).

Rollout plan: feature-flag guarded; staged rollout on runtime-1.20 images in canary cluster, then gradual ramp to serving pool with telemetry verification. Provide emergency kill-switch that disables overlay at runtime.
acceptance_criteria: Design doc reviewed and approved by runtime and serving teams (design review notes linked)
Prototype kernel adapter merged to runtime repo with overlay ABI tests
Bench harness demonstrates >= 30% restored-bytes reduction on at least two representative sparse workloads
End-to-end load test shows no regression in 95th latency and >=10% improvement in 99.9th latency for target workloads
Per-tenant accounting and quota integration completed; safety tests for tenant isolation pass
Feature flag and rollback path validated; rollout playbook documented
updates: 2026-02-17: Kickoff sync with serving/infra. Agreed Bloom size budget of 128 bytes/page as starting point. Decided reservoir will be per-tenant with soft quotas.

2026-02-24: Prototype overlay descriptor sketch done. Spike shows we can encode overlay in 16 bytes + N pointers. Posting design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Bloom-guided+Lazy+Restore

2026-03-02: Kernel adapter prototype (sparse path) in branch feature/bloom-overlay. Initial microbench shows sparse kernel overhead roughly +8% compute vs dense kernel but restores bytes reduced ~55% on synthetic sparse workload.

2026-03-05: Design review with PM/SEC. SEC requested explicit audit logging for restored keys — added to acceptance criteria. Also flagged tenant metadata exposure risk; changed Bloom to contain hashed slot ids only.
2026-03-09: Integration test failing due to CUDA allocator fragmentation when reserving ephemeral reservoir ranges. Diego investigating; potential fix via pooled-suballocator (ENG-80359 referenced).
